name: Tlingit
info: The Tlingit, or Lingít, are an Indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest Coast, Alaska Natives and First Nations in Canada, known for their matrilineal clans, crest art and a hunting, fishing and gathering life built on rich fisheries.

facts.homeland: Lingít Aaní, the Land of the Tlingit: from Yakutat south through the Alaskan Panhandle and the Alexander Archipelago, and inland along the Alsek, Tatshenshini, Chilkat, Taku and Stikine rivers to Atlin, Teslin and Tagish Lakes in northwestern British Columbia and the southern Yukon
facts.period: Human culture with elements related to the Tlingit from around 10,000 years ago; first contact with Russian explorers in 1741 and Spanish in 1775; the 1862 smallpox epidemic; conversions to Orthodox Christianity between 1886 and 1895; today federally recognized tribes in Alaska and First Nations in Canada
facts.known: matrilineal clans within the Raven and Eagle moieties; heraldic crests on totem poles, canoes and house posts; cedar plank clan houses; at.oow, inherited objects held in trust; a rich oratory tradition; Chilkat and Ravenstail weaving; salmon fisheries
facts.sources: The Tlingit's own traditions and present-day communities; Russian sources such as Grigory Shelikhov's 1796 map; ethnographies such as those by Frederica de Laguna, George Thornton Emmons and Sergei Kan; Swanton's Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909); genetic studies of HLA genes

t: Tlingit society is divided into two moieties, the Raven and the Eagle, made up of clans in which descent and inheritance pass through the mother's line.
The 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic killed about 60% of the Mainland Tlingit and 37% of the Island Tlingit.
Tribes, institutions and linguists are working to revitalize the Tlingit language, which has an estimated 200 to 400 speakers in the United States and 100 in Canada.
dyk: The name Lingít means 'People of the Tides', while the old Russian name for them, Koloshi, came from a Sugpiaq-Alutiiq word for the labret worn by women.

sections.origins:
Indigenous peoples of various cultures have lived continuously in what is now Alaska for thousands of years, and from them came the Tlingit. Human culture with elements related to the Tlingit arose around 10,000 years ago near the mouths of the Skeena and Nass Rivers. Tlingit culture and society developed in the temperate rainforest of the southeast Alaskan coast and the Alexander Archipelago. Their own name, Lingít, means "People of the Tides".

The Tlingit speak the Tlingit language, which forms an independent branch of the Na-Dene family and has a complex grammar and sound system with several rare sounds. Genetic studies of HLA genes link some Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast, especially the Tlingit, to the Ainu of Japan, and the scientists suggest that their main ancestors can be traced to Palaeolithic groups in Southern Siberia.

The Tlingit live in four broad divisions that follow differences of environment, dialect and food: the Southern Tlingit south of Frederick Sound, the Northern Tlingit from Frederick Sound to Cape Spencer and Lynn Canal, the Inland Tlingit of the lakes and the Taku River, and the Gulf Coast Tlingit north of Cape Spencer. These academic divisions match the Tlingit's own sense of themselves.
sections.society:
Family and kinship stand at the centre of Tlingit life. Society is divided into two moieties, the Raven and the Eagle, which are divided into many clans and these into lineages or house groups. Children are born into their mother's clan, and property and hereditary roles pass through the mother's line. Wealth and economic power mark rank, but so do generosity and proper behaviour. Like other Northwest Coast peoples, the Tlingit practised hereditary slavery, extensively, until the United States outlawed it.

The Tlingit have kept a complex way of life based on the semi-sedentary management of fisheries. No food receives as much emphasis as salmon, with seal and game close behind. Halibut, shellfish and seaweed come in spring, seal and salmon in late spring and summer, berries such as salmonberry and soapberry in summer, and sea otters are hunted in autumn; herring and eulachon are eaten fresh or dried. In the forests they hunt deer, bear and mountain goats. Living only on "beach food" is held a sign of poverty. Today many Tlingit men work in fishing and women in canneries or the handicraft trade.
sections.beliefs:
Tlingit thought and belief, though never formally codified, has been a well-organised philosophical and religious system shaping how people see and act in the world. The Tlingit were traditionally animists, and a central tenet is the reincarnation of both humans and animals. Hunters purified themselves ritually before a hunt. Shamans, mostly men, cured diseases, influenced the weather, helped in hunting, foretold the future and protected people from witchcraft. Shamans and their families had to abstain from all food gathered from the beach, and men might avoid it before battle in the belief that it would weaken them.

Between 1886 and 1895, as their shamans could not treat smallpox and other Old World diseases, many Tlingit converted to Orthodox Christianity, whose liturgy Russian missionaries had translated into Tlingit. It has been argued that they saw Orthodoxy as a way of resisting assimilation to the "American way of life", associated with Presbyterianism. After the coming of Christianity the old belief system began to erode, but today some young Tlingit look to traditional religion for inspiration and identity, and many contemporary Tlingit reconcile Christianity with traditional culture.
sections.arts:
Art and spirituality run through nearly every part of Tlingit culture, so that even everyday objects such as spoons and storage boxes are decorated and carry spiritual power and history. Clans and lineages have heraldic crests, which are displayed on totem poles, canoes, feast dishes, house posts, weavings and jewellery. Tlingit families pass down at.oow, blankets and other objects that represent trust: only a Tlingit can inherit one, though it may be given to someone trusted, who cares for it without owning it.

The Tlingit historically built cedar plank houses, which they now call clan houses. These were square or rectangular, with foundations that allowed belongings to be stored under the floor, and it is said that no adhesive, nails or other fastenings were used; their fronts carried designs and totem poles showing the clan and moiety of the makers. A rich tradition of oratory is central to the culture. Weaving and carving continue today, in the work of Chilkat and Ravenstail weavers such as Jennie Thlunaut, Anna Brown Ehlers and Clarissa Rizal and carvers such as Nathan Jackson and Amos Wallace, and in wood carvings and baskets made for use and for sale.
sections.exchange:
Travelling up the great rivers that cross the Coast and Saint Elias Mountains, the Tlingit built wide trade networks with the Athabascan peoples of the interior and often married among them; some settled around Atlin, Teslin and Tagish Lakes. The Coastal Tlingit controlled one of the mountain passes into the Yukon interior. Tlingit groups trade among themselves and with neighbouring communities, and they share land with Athabascan peoples such as the Tahltan, Kaska and Tagish. The Kaigani Haida moved to the southern end of Prince of Wales Island just before the first European encounters.

The Tlingit first met Europeans in 1741, when Russian explorers arrived, followed by the Spanish in 1775. The Tlingit kept their independence, but they suffered from epidemics of smallpox and other diseases brought by Europeans. The 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic killed about 60% of the Mainland Tlingit and 37% of the Island Tlingit. Missionaries followed, and Orthodox and Presbyterian churches came to stand for different paths under American rule, the latter linked with assimilation.
sections.legacy:
The Tlingit today are both Alaska Natives and First Nations in Canada. In Alaska there are federally recognized tribes, among them the Central Council of the Tlingit & Haida Indian Tribes, the Sitka Tribe of Alaska and the Yakutat Tlingit Tribe. Alaska has no Tlingit reservations: the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act set up regional corporations with land holdings instead, and Sealaska Corporation serves the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian. In Canada the Carcross/Tagish First Nation, the Taku River Tlingit First Nation and the Teslin Tlingit Council have reserves. Tlingit people take part in Alaska's commercial economy and live within their historical homelands.

The language now has an estimated 200 to 400 speakers in the United States and 100 in Canada, all bilingual in English. Sealaska Heritage Institute, Goldbelt Heritage Institute and the University of Alaska Southeast run Tlingit language programmes, and community classes are held in Klukwan and Angoon. Tlingit people have been prominent in civil rights, scholarship and the arts, among them the civil rights advocates Elizabeth Peratrovich and Tillie Paul, the scholar Nora Marks Dauenhauer, the elder Walter Soboleff and the glass artist Preston Singletary.

summary: The Tlingit are an Indigenous people of southeast Alaska, British Columbia and the Yukon, organised in matrilineal clans of the Raven and Eagle moieties and known for their crest art, clan houses and fisheries. They survived epidemics that killed most of the mainland people in 1862 and today live as federally recognized tribes and First Nations, working to revive their language.
